text: Everything from the first four chapters funnels into this one deliverable: a written report following the same structure you learned to read critically back in Chapter 1, now written from the other side.

This lesson covers the methods, results, limitations, and conclusions structure and what belongs in each section, why the limitations section is not an apology but a core, expected part of a credible report, how to turn your experiment summary into each section, and common write-up mistakes that undercut otherwise solid work.

Methods states exactly what you built and ran — circuit, technique, parameters, hardware, named specifically. Results holds the actual data and claim-by-claim analysis — numbers, not adjectives; 'the reduction was 0.155' belongs here, 'mitigation worked really well' does not. Limitations covers what your result does and doesn't show, including any confound, any specification choice you made yourself, and any scope you deliberately didn't cover. Conclusions ties your honest, bounded takeaway explicitly back to your hypothesis's specific claims.

In a worked excerpt: we measured a GHZ-fidelity error reduction of 0.155 at three qubits and 0.120 at five qubits, using zero-noise extrapolation with Richardson extrapolation, on a named device and date. The five-qubit reduction is about 22.6 percent smaller than the three-qubit one, supporting both claims of the original hypothesis — that mitigation helps at both qubit counts, and that the improvement shrinks as qubit count increases.

A thin or missing limitations section was one of the overstatement red flags you learned to spot reading other people's papers — don't reproduce that flaw in your own report. A strong limitations section is a sign of a credible researcher, not a weak result, because it tells the reader exactly how far to trust the conclusion. Common mistakes include reporting adjectives instead of numbers, burying limitations in one throwaway sentence, and letting the conclusion generalize beyond this specific device and calibration window.

Next lesson builds the presentation version of this same work — for a technical audience that could ask you hard questions about your methods, which needs a genuinely different structure than the written report.
